# /rite:review-all — the whole review queue, independent

Arguments: `$ARGUMENTS`

Review only: never change code, docs or the tasks' work. Each task gets the treatment of
`/rite:review` — a fresh reviewer that **measures instead of reads** — and the run ends with every task
of the queue reviewed.

## Steps

1. `rite begin review --cycle <cycle> --no-claim --json` resolves the cycle and its config. The batch:
   the task IDs given, or the queue **now** (`rite batch-plan all --kind review --cycle <cycle>
   --json`); tasks done mid-run wait for the next run: a batch that grows never ends. Exit `1` with
   "no selectable review" → the queue is empty: report and stop.
2. **Read the plan.** Reviewers edit nothing, so files and dependencies never separate them; a wave
   holds tasks that share no serialized resource, at most `[limits].review_parallel` of them
   (`parallel_cap`). One wave of one task each means the run is sequential: say why (cap `1`, or
   the resource each pair shares). With `--plan`, show items, conflicts and waves, and stop: nothing
   is written.
3. **Each wave**: `rite begin review --cycle <cycle> --id <ID> --json` per task — it opens the
   review's clock (`review_started_at`) — then one fresh `rite:rite-reviewer` per task, **in parallel, in one message** — never this
   context. Give each the facts `/rite:review` gives: the payload of `rite context <ID> --json`, the
   repository it works in (`item.repo_dir` when given, else the root), the CLI invocation, the task's
   `done_commit`, and the instruction "Review this task per your procedure and return findings in your
   format." Do not tell any what you think of the work, nor what another reviewer found. Commit
   nothing while reviewers run: they measure HEAD.
4. **Screen the findings** of each report. Keep one only if it carries a runnable evidence command and
   its output, and at least one of its commands runs on the working tree (a pinned revision cannot
   turn green). Do not re-review, soften or add findings of your own; list what you dropped, with the
   reason.
5. **Merge duplicates across reviews** — this wave's and the earlier ones': two kept findings with the
   same evidence command and the same files are one root cause, so one fix, its origin the lowest
   task ID; every review that found it lists that fix. Findings that only look alike stay apart.
6. **Serially, in task order**, close the wave before the next starts:
   - one fix per kept finding: `rite new-fix --cycle <cycle> --origin <ID> --title "<title>" --severity
     <critical|high|medium|low> --json`, then fill the body sections (Problem, Evidence, Root cause,
     Fix, Files, Verification) — never its frontmatter or the JSON state. A merged fix lists every
     task's evidence. In Evidence the CLI is `sh "$RITE_HOME/bin/rite"`, never a resolved plugin
     path. A finding about a phase with no entry in the profile's phase checks is itself a `medium` fix;
   - `rite mark-reviewed <ID> [--fixes <FIX-ID>,…] --json` — one commit per task, also with no finding,
     because a review without a record leaves the task to be selected again. In a local cycle it writes
     the files and commits nothing.
   A run cut short keeps every closed wave; the next run takes only what is left in the queue.
7. After the last wave: `rite check --quick --cycle <cycle> --json`, then `rite status --cycle <cycle>
   --json`: no task of the batch may remain in `review_queue`. One that does is named with the reason
   (reviewer failed, `mark-reviewed` refused) — never left unsaid.

## Report

Waves with their task IDs, and why the run was parallel or sequential (cap, shared resources) · per
task: `done_commit`, the four universal verdicts in one line, phase checks (pending ones with the task they wait on), fixes opened, the commit
SHA or "local cycle" · merged fixes and the tasks behind each · dropped findings with reasons · tasks
left in the queue, if any · what to run next (usually `/rite:fix-all`).

## The CLI

Every state read and every state change goes through it: hand-written bookkeeping drifts.

```sh
sh "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/rite" <subcommand> [args] --json
```

Find it in that order, never by searching the disk: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/rite`,
`$RITE_HOME/bin/rite`, `rite` on `PATH`; none → ask the user. Below, `rite <sub>` means that
invocation, run inside the repository or with `--root <repo>`; prefer `--json`.

Exit codes: `0` ok · `1` failure or nothing selected (stderr names the rule; no `--force` unless
asked) · `3` no `rite.toml` — stop and tell the user to run `/rite:init`.

Reply in the JSON's `session_language`; empty → the session's language.

## State

The cycle's `progress.json` (meta + tasks) and `fixes.json` are the only state; item files hold prose
and their `id`; the tables in the progress and fixes files are views the CLI renders from the JSON.

- `rite begin <kind> [--cycle C] [--id ID] --json` resolves the cycle, takes the item and returns its
  paths, the config digest and the commit template. Idempotent.
- `rite finish <ID> [--sha S] --json` closes the item from its work commit, runs `check --quick` and
  names the next one. Two commits per item — the work, then the CLI's record (a commit cannot hold its
  own SHA). No work commit, only a document outside git: `--no-repo --reason "…"`, never borrow HEAD.
- Others: `rite mark <ID> blocked|skipped --reason "…" --commit`, `mark-reviewed <ID> [--fixes …]`,
  `mark-stale <FIX> --reason "…"`, `rebind <ID> --sha <commit>` after a squash.
- A fix blocked by the environment adds `--unblocked-by "<command that passes once it is there>"`.
  Partial work: commit what is coherent, then `mark blocked` with the `--reason` naming what is
  missing and the partial SHA — never `close` (not done), never `mark-stale` (the symptom is there).
- A **local cycle** (`"local": true`) writes the same fields and commits nothing, by design; never
  commit its documents yourself.

- Planning fields: `rite set <ID> --files a,b --resources r --depends-on <IDs>`; the cycle's `order`,
  `ticket`, `plan`: `rite set-cycle --cycle C --order <IDs>`. The only fields you write.

Never edit `progress.json` / `fixes.json` (the guard refuses it), never put fields back into an item's
frontmatter, never edit between `<!-- rite:begin … -->` and `<!-- rite:end -->`, never invent an ID.

## Evidence

- **Measure, do not read**: a claim counts only if you ran its command here; logs are leads.
- **Every number has a tool**: quote its versioned command beside it.
- **Control before test**: a checker must be seen to fail, Evidence to pass once fixed — a pinned git
  revision or an old log documents, never verifies.
- **Reproduce before fixing** (`rite reproduce <FIX> --json`, `--scratch` if it writes files):
  `REPRODUCED` → fix it · `NOT REPRODUCED` (`why: ok`, output contradicts the Evidence) → *stale*
  (`rite mark-stale`) · else `CANNOT RUN` (other `why`, `cannot_decide`: a `shell_error`,
  `missing_path` or `timed_out`) → an agent or a person, never *stale*. An exit code is not a verdict.
- **Negative results are results**: "X fails, because Y (command, output)".
- **Gates**: `rite gates [--id <ID>] --json`. Red means not done: fix it, or stop and report its
  output.

## Repositories

If `rite begin` gave no `commit.repo_dir`, ignore this section.

An item's work lands in its repository, `commit.repo_dir`: run its commands and git there (`git -C
<repo_dir> …`, a batch's `status` and `stash` too) and read its paths relative to it. One item, one
repository. Rite's documents are never staged there; in a workspace every cycle is local.

## Reporting

**At most 15 lines.** IDs, commands, measured numbers, SHAs, and what the user must decide. Do not
re-tell what the item file already says, and do not paste output that was not decisive.
